speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Cash receipts reflect all the cash that comes in.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Every year, the Department of Statistics (DOS) reports our cash receipts and indicates whether we have a cash surplus or cash deficit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: But not all our cash receipts constitute revenue available for spending.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The largest difference between our cash receipts and revenue comes from the sale of state land.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Such proceeds from land sales do not generate fresh revenue.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: They are simply a transformation of one asset to another – when land is sold, the asset is converted to cash.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: State land that are not due for immediate development are typically leased out for interim use.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This yields revenue for the Government too, in the form of rental income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: So, selling land does not increase the Government’s revenue, and if we were to spend all the proceeds from land, it would deplete our store of wealth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Think of a family that has a house.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: So long as the family owns the house, it can rent out some of the empty rooms to generate income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: But if the family sells the house and uses the proceeds for day-to-day expenditure, it will soon have nothing left.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: However, if it invests the proceeds of sale wisely, it will still have the original sale proceeds, plus a constant stream of income from those proceeds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This income can then be used partially for expenditure and partially re-invested to help sustain both present and future members of the family.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Likewise, for Government budgeting, land sales proceeds are not considered part of our revenue and cannot be directly used for expenditure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Instead, they are invested and part of the investment income is used to support the spending needs of Singaporeans via the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This is only possible because of the prudent and disciplined approach we have taken to building and protecting both our land and financial reserves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: In a recent social media post, the Workers' Party claimed that there is no need to raise GST because of the cash surplus.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: As I have explained, this claim is inaccurate and misleading.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Under the Constitution, the Government is required to balance the Budget over the term of government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And so, I wanted to ask the Minister whether this requirement, does it lead to the Government typically being more conservative in the Budget during the early parts of the term, and then, distribute and spend a bit more in the later part of the term?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Do we have that phenomenon because of that Constitution requirements?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government seeks to run a balanced Budget over the term of government by spending prudently within the limits of its annual revenues and any accumulated surpluses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government has generally adhered to this in line with the Constitutional requirement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In general, this means that we avoid running deficits early in the term of government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is not only to avoid a draw on past reserves, which should be reserved for exceptional situations, it also helps the Government to preserve fiscal headroom to deal with unexpected spending needs during its term of government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, in the event of a major crisis, the Government is prepared to run a deficit and seek a draw on past reserves regardless of which part of the term it happens to be in.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If and when we have unexpected surpluses, we have used them in three ways.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, we share some of the surpluses with Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In financial year (FY) 2018, we distributed up to $300 per Singaporean through the SG Bonus following an exceptional surplus in FY2017 due to unexpected market movements that resulted in higher Statutory Board contributions from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, we save for anticipated future needs such as the Railway Infrastructure Fund and the Coastal and Flood Protection Fund.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Last, any unutilised fiscal space becomes part of past reserves, which is invested and supports future spending needs via the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A GST hike alone could lead to a lower path for GDP and private consumption, and limited external adjustment, relative to using more of the available fiscal space".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And, I think, again in 2019, the IMF also said that, "Singapore has tended to overperform with respect to its fiscal rule of a balanced Budget over the political cycle, contributing to a large build-up of net assets suggesting that Singapore has substantial fiscal space." Mr Speaker, if we look at the situation in 2018 versus today, where we have COVID-19 in terms of what is impacting the cost of living, the question that I have is, is raising a regressive tax such as the GST really the best option for us in terms of raising revenues?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Could there be other options that could be explored, for example, looking at the NIRC framework again?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And this also brings me to the second clarification, which I also raised during the debate earlier in February, in that if you look at our reserves position today, we are looking at having drawn down about 20 years' worth of surpluses – some Members have said that it is about 10 years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Where do our reserve stand today versus, say, last 10 years or five years?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That would help us to adequately frame the context of this GST rise as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He opened by saying that we had discussed this topic during the Budget.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: During the Budget, the Workers' Party, touched peripherally on the Budget.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I believe Mr Louis Chua mentioned land sales.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But what the Workers' Party did not say during the Budget debate, was what they had said in their social media post.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, effectively, in their social media post, what they are really saying is that the Government is not setting out the correct fiscal position.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, essentially, in the social media post, what the Workers' Party had done was to point just to cash surpluses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And as I explained earlier, you cannot look just at cash surpluses to understand the fiscal position.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You also need to look whether or not all of that constitutes revenue under our budgeting rules.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And as for the reasons that I explained earlier, it does not.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that was the first point that I wanted to respond to the Member Mr Louis Chua.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, the second point that he raised I think – well, he went through quite a lot of things but I think that the question that he ultimately came back to was, is the raising of GST the best option?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think after going through what the IMF said and so on, that was the question, and is it time to look at the NIRC formula again?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This has been explained in some detail by the Deputy Prime Minister during the Budget.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, this question should have been brought up during the Budget because then it would have given the Government the opportunity to explain the position.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But in summary, we all know, we are so badly constrained, because of COVID-19, we already have to go into actual reserves, we have to dip into actual reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is no longer just a question of taking from income on the reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are squeezed on the corporate tax front.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because of the economic situation, you can have a scenario where even your personal income tax is going to be affected.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is no magic to this formula but it is a fair formula: 50% for today's generation and another 50% for tomorrow's generation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The first point is that, during my speech, I did set out, in terms of the revenues and expenditures as well as how I arrived at some of these numbers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: But I think the question is also about whether or not, looking at this NRIC framework, that is something that we can revisit again.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I agree with Minister that, because of COVID-19, this has actually impacted a lot of Singaporeans, a lot of corporates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: And all the more, I think a regressive tax such as GST, should be something that we should reconsider.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Because while the Assurance Package could offset the impact of the increase of 2% for a number of years, I think this is going to stick with them basically for the rest of their lives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, given the impact of COVID-19 and all on the livelihoods of Singaporeans, the man on the street, could we not look at the NIRC framework again, as perhaps another measure, given where our reserves have been.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In essence, what the Member is saying is this: he is saying that you have the NIRC framework, can we not re-look it?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We all know that things are not set in stone always, but we also know that when it comes to a matter of public policy and when you have frameworks, especially frameworks for expenditure, you cannot just chop and change every other year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it would make instructive reading for Members and anybody who is interested in this, to actually go back to the time when we did set up the framework.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This was dealt with in the speech by the Prime Minister when we did the amendments and it is a very instructive speech.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He said, "Parliament is considering an important Constitutional amendment to our reserves framework.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The immediate issue before us is just a formula change.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: How much income can the Government draw from the past reserves?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The new formula will allow us to spend somewhat more.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the deeper significance of this amendment is to establish a more sustainable and equitable basis for spending out of the investment returns.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Sustainable and equitable, so that we have resources which can benefit both the present generation and future generations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While we spend for our needs, we also put aside a solid buffer for contingencies, for the proverbial rainy day.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the most fundamental significance of this amendment is that it reaffirms the importance of protecting our reserves...".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In that speech, the Prime Minister takes us through the history of how originally it was just protecting the principal amount; then after that, we had the NII framework and we spent a 100% of that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I cannot say whether 50 or 100 years from now, we change that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But we should not do is just every year or every two years, when something looks like the the scenario will need a bit more expenditure, we just change the framework so easily.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The framework took a long time to come to and was very carefully considered and thought through, tried and tested, many steps.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And once we have a framework in place, you should not easily change it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But, and this is the real point, which I have mentioned, we know that there is an impact on lower income and middle income, which is why we have taken the steps that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Member talks about how the buffer or the Assurance Package will last for five years and 10 years, but the impact will be longer than that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And also, over five and 10 years, there is time for incomes to rise.
